  3. A composite kernel with RBF, constant, and periodic components

  4. A Matérn kernel with different smoothness parameters

Each choice makes different assumptions about the underlying physical processes. The RBF kernel assumes smooth, aperiodic variations. The periodic kernel assumes regular, repeating patterns. The composite kernel allows several processes to operate at the same time.

A further difficulty is that a more complex kernel can fit the data at least as well as a simpler one. A composite kernel with many components can model the same patterns as a simple kernel, and more. Without a penalty for complexity, we would choose the most flexible option, and this leads to overfitting.

Gaussian processes address this problem with Bayesian model comparison. For each candidate kernel structure \(\mathcal{M}_i\), we can compute the marginal likelihood \[ p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{X}, \mathcal{M}_i) = \int p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathcal{M}_i) p(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \mathcal{M}_i) \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}. \] Here \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta} | \mathcal{M}_i)\) is the prior over the hyperparameters of model \(\mathcal{M}_i\). In Section 14.9 the marginal likelihood is conditioned on fixed hyperparameters, whereas this one averages over them.

In practice, we typically approximate this integral by the marginal likelihood at the optimal hyperparameters \[ p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{X}, \mathcal{M}_i) \approx p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\theta}^*_i). \] Here \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^*_i\) maximizes the marginal likelihood of model \(\mathcal{M}_i\). The full integral also penalizes models with more hyperparameters, because it averages the likelihood over a larger space of hyperparameter values. The maximum drops the penalty for the number of hyperparameters. A kernel that contains a simpler kernel as a limit therefore does not score lower.

The marginal likelihood still penalizes flexible covariance through the determinant term that we examined in Section 14.9. Adding a covariance component raises the determinant when the other parameters stay fixed. For kernels that do not contain one another, the determinant term is the only penalty for complexity. Kernel selection thus adds a second step to hyperparameter optimization. We first optimize the hyperparameters of each structure and then compare the structures with the same objective function.

Information Criteria

The marginal likelihood is one Bayesian approach to model comparison. But we sometimes want additional safeguards against overfitting, or we must work with approximations to the full Bayesian treatment. Information criteria add an explicit penalty for the number of hyperparameters, which the maximized marginal likelihood lacks.

Two simple options are the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) and the Akaike information criterion (AIC) of Section 11.8, which are defined as \[\begin{aligned} \text{BIC} &= -2\ln(\hat{L}) + P\ln(N) \\ \text{AIC} &= -2\ln(\hat{L}) + 2P. \end{aligned}\] Here \(\hat{L}\) is the maximized marginal likelihood, \(P\) is the number of hyperparameters, and \(N\) is the sample size. We choose the model with the lowest criterion value.

The BIC penalty depends on the sample size, so BIC penalizes complexity more for large datasets. For Gaussian processes, these criteria are particularly useful when we compare models with very different numbers of hyperparameters. A simple RBF kernel has 2 to 3 hyperparameters, while a complex composite kernel might have 10 or more.

Cross-Validation

Cross-validation is another approach. It measures the predictive performance directly and does not rely on theoretical penalties for complexity. For Gaussian processes, we typically use \(K\)-fold cross-validation (Section 4.7). It divides the dataset into \(K\) subsets, called folds, trains on \(K-1\) folds, and tests on the remaining fold. We average a score over the \(K\) test folds.

A suitable score for GPs is the negative log predictive density (NLPD) of a test fold, which is \[ \text{NLPD} = -\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}|} \sum_{(\mathbf{x}_i, t_i) \in \mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}} \ln p(t_i | \mathbf{x}_i, \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}). \]Here \(|\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}|\) is the number of test points of the fold, and \(p(t_i | \mathbf{x}_i, \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}})\) is the density that the GP trained on \(\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\) assigns to \(t_i\). A lower NLPD means better predictions. NLPD evaluates both the point predictions and the uncertainty estimates, which suits Gaussian processes, where uncertainty quantification is an important advantage. A model with confident but wrong predictions is penalized more heavily than a model that expresses appropriate uncertainty.

Cross-validation for GPs can be computationally expensive, because each fold requires training a model on approximately \((K-1)/K \times N\) data points. However, it gives direct evidence of the predictive performance, and it can reveal overfitting that marginal likelihood comparisons alone may not show. We use the marginal likelihood to find the model that best explains the observed data. We use cross-validation to find the model that is most likely to perform well on future observations.

In practice, effective model selection for Gaussian processes combines several approaches. A typical workflow starts with simple kernels (RBF, periodic, linear) and compares them with the marginal likelihood. We then construct composite models by combining the promising components. Cross-validation provides the final validation of the predictive performance.

For astronomical applications, we focus on kernel combinations that correspond to the plausible physical processes of Section 14.3, instead of testing many possible combinations. This reduces the computational burden while keeping the models scientifically interpretable.

14.11 Gaussian Process Classification

Gaussian process regression predicts continuous outputs, such as stellar brightness or radial velocity. Many astronomical problems need classification instead, which assigns an object to a discrete category. We might classify stars by spectral type, separate stars from galaxies in photometric surveys, or identify different types of variable objects from their light curves. Can we extend Gaussian processes to classification? The step resembles the move from linear regression to logistic regression (Section 7.3), because we again need a special technique for binary outcomes.

In regression, the observations are continuous values that we model as Gaussian random variables. We write \(t_i = f(\mathbf{x}_i) + \epsilon_i\), where \(f\) is the latent function and \(\epsilon_i\) is Gaussian noise. In classification, the observations are discrete class labels, typically 0 and 1 for binary problems. We cannot write \(t_i = f(\mathbf{x}_i) + \epsilon_i\) for class labels, because a continuous function plus continuous noise gives continuous values. Such values cannot be the discrete labels 0 and 1. We need a different relationship between the latent function and the observed outcomes.

The solution, familiar from logistic regression, is a link function, such as the sigmoid, that connects continuous function values to class probabilities. We assume an underlying continuous function \(a(\mathbf{x})\), often called the “logit” or “score” function, which determines the class probabilities through the link function. We keep the Gaussian process for the latent function, which can take any real value, and we handle the discrete observations through an appropriate likelihood.

From Linear to Nonlinear Boundaries

To understand the motivation for Gaussian process classification, we first recall the limitation of logistic regression (Section 7.5). Logistic regression models the class probability as \[ p(t=1|\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})), \] where \(\sigma(a) = 1/(1+e^{-a})\) is the sigmoid function and \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\) represents the feature mapping.

The main limitation concerns the decision boundary, the set of points where \(p(t=1|\mathbf{x}) = 0.5\). It lies where \(\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}) = 0\), which defines a hyperplane in feature space. This restricts us to boundaries that are linear in the feature space. Even with carefully designed features, many real classification problems need nonlinear boundaries that are hard to describe with explicit feature mappings.

Consider the separation of stars from galaxies by their photometric colors. The true boundary between the two classes in color space is often curved and complex. It depends on redshift effects, stellar populations and observational selection functions. A linear classifier might capture the overall separation but miss important substructure.

Gaussian process classification lifts this restriction. It replaces the linear function \(\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\) with a nonlinear function \(a(\mathbf{x})\) that follows a Gaussian process prior \[ a(\mathbf{x}) \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')). \]

For simplicity, we use a zero mean function, which can be generalized. The sigmoid turns the logit \(a(\mathbf{x})\) into a probability, so that \[ p(t=1|\mathbf{x}, a) = \sigma(a(\mathbf{x})). \]

The kernel function gives the flexibility to learn complex decision boundaries, and the probabilistic model gives the uncertainty of each classification. Figure 14.10 compares the decision boundary and the predicted class probability of a linear classifier with those of a Gaussian process classifier.

The model passes information from the input features to the class labels in three steps.

  1. The Gaussian process maps the input features \(\mathbf{x}_i\) to latent function values \(a_i = a(\mathbf{x}_i)\). These latent values can take any real number and represent the “score” for class membership before the conversion to probabilities.

  2. The sigmoid function converts the latent values to class probabilities \(p_i = \sigma(a_i)\), which lie between 0 and 1.

  3. We observe discrete class labels \(t_i\) that are sampled from Bernoulli distributions with probabilities \(p_i\).

In the first step, the kernel function encodes our assumptions about which inputs should receive similar scores. The uncertainty of the latent function, given by the posterior variance of the Gaussian process, carries over to the class probability through the sigmoid. Near a decision boundary, where \(a(\mathbf{x}) \approx 0\), small changes in the latent function produce large changes in the class probability. The model then expresses high uncertainty. Far from the boundary, where \(|a(\mathbf{x})|\) is large, the sigmoid saturates, and the uncertainty of the latent function has less effect on the class probability. Figure 14.11 shows the three steps in panel (e) and this effect in panel (d).

This propagation of uncertainty makes Gaussian process classification useful for astronomical applications that must identify objects that are difficult to classify. Instead of forcing a discrete classification, the model can express uncertainty about ambiguous cases. Follow-up observations can then target the cases where they help most.

The nonlinear link function makes exact Bayesian inference intractable. In GP regression, a Gaussian likelihood keeps the posterior Gaussian, a property called conjugacy (Section 5.2). The sigmoid creates a non-Gaussian posterior that needs approximation techniques. This complexity is the price of nonlinear decision boundaries.

14.12 The Predictive Distribution in GP Classification

The computation of predictions needs more care, because the latent values relate nonlinearly to the class probabilities. Our goal is the probability that a new test point \(\mathbf{x}_*\) belongs to class 1, given the training data \(\{\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}\}\). This is the predictive distribution \[ p(t_*=1|\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}). \]

To see why classification is harder than regression, we follow the four steps of the inference.

  1. We observe inputs \(\mathbf{X}\) and discrete class labels \(\mathbf{t} \in \{0,1\}^N\).

  2. We use these data to infer the distribution of the logit values \(\mathbf{a}\) at the training points.

  3. The trained Gaussian process predicts the logit value \(a_*\) at the test point \(\mathbf{x}_*\).

  4. We convert the predicted logit to a class probability with the sigmoid function.

The problem comes from the sigmoid of step 2. We observe discrete labels, which connect to the latent function through the nonlinear sigmoid. The posterior over the latent function values is then non-Gaussian, and we cannot compute it analytically.

To formalize the challenge, we apply the sum and product rules of probability to the predictive distribution. We do not observe the logit values directly, so we marginalize over all possible values of \(a_*\) and obtain \[ p(t_*=1|\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) = \int p(t_*=1|a_*) p(a_*|\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) \mathrm{d}a_*. \]

The first term in the integral is straightforward, \(p(t_*=1|a_*) = \sigma(a_*)\). The challenge is the second term, \(p(a_*|\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t})\), which requires us to infer the latent function distribution from discrete observations.

The sum rule again, now over the latent values \(\mathbf{a}\) at the training points, gives \[ p(a_*|\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) = \int p(a_*|\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}) p(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{a}. \]

The first factor is a standard GP prediction \[ p(a_*|\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}) = \mathcal{N}(a_*|\mu_{a_*|\mathbf{a}}, \sigma_{a_*|\mathbf{a}}^2), \] where the mean and variance follow from Gaussian conditioning, as in Section 14.7 without noise.

The problematic factor is \(p(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t})\), the posterior distribution of the latent function values given the observed class labels. Bayes’ rule gives \[ p(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{a}) p(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{X})}{p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{X})}. \]

The prior \(p(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{X}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{K})\) is Gaussian. The likelihood \(p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{a}) = \prod_{i=1}^N \sigma(a_i)^{t_i}(1-\sigma(a_i))^{1-t_i}\) is a product of sigmoid functions. A Gaussian prior times this non-Gaussian likelihood is no longer Gaussian.

The Laplace Approximation

We cannot remove the sigmoid, so we approximate the non-Gaussian posterior \(p(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t})\) by a Gaussian. We use the Laplace approximation, which we introduced in Sections 9.3 and 9.4 for Bayesian logistic regression.

The Laplace approximation has three steps.

  1. We find the mode \(\mathbf{a}_{\text{MAP}}\) of the posterior distribution, the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate.

  2. We compute the Hessian matrix, the matrix of second derivatives, of the negative log posterior at this mode.

  3. We construct a Gaussian approximation from the mode and the Hessian.

To find the mode, we maximize the log posterior, which is given by \[ \ln p(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) = \sum_{i=1}^N [t_i \ln \sigma(a_i) + (1-t_i) \ln (1-\sigma(a_i))] - \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{a} + \text{const}. \]

The first term of the log posterior is the log likelihood of the labels, and the second term comes from the Gaussian prior. We set the gradient to zero. Both the gradient and the Hessian use the derivative of the sigmoid, which Section 7.7 derived. For the likelihood term, the partial derivative with respect to each \(a_i\) is \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial}{\partial a_i} [t_i \ln \sigma(a_i) + (1-t_i) \ln (1-\sigma(a_i))] &= t_i \frac{\sigma'(a_i)}{\sigma(a_i)} + (1-t_i) \frac{-\sigma'(a_i)}{1-\sigma(a_i)}. \end{aligned}\]

Using \(\sigma'(a_i) = \sigma(a_i)(1-\sigma(a_i))\), this simplifies to \[\begin{aligned} &= t_i \frac{\sigma(a_i)(1-\sigma(a_i))}{\sigma(a_i)} - (1-t_i) \frac{\sigma(a_i)(1-\sigma(a_i))}{1-\sigma(a_i)} \\ &= t_i(1-\sigma(a_i)) - (1-t_i)\sigma(a_i) \\ &= t_i - t_i\sigma(a_i) - \sigma(a_i) + t_i\sigma(a_i) \\ &= t_i - \sigma(a_i). \end{aligned}\]

Setting the full gradient to zero gives \[ \nabla_{\mathbf{a}} \ln p(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) = \mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{a}) - \mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}, \] where \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{a}) = [\sigma(a_1), \sigma(a_2), \ldots, \sigma(a_N)]^T\).

The sigmoid is nonlinear, so this equation has no closed-form solution. We solve it iteratively by gradient ascent with learning rate \(\eta\), which gives the update \[ \mathbf{a}^{(\tau+1)} = \mathbf{a}^{(\tau)} + \eta \left(\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{a}^{(\tau)}) - \mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{a}^{(\tau)}\right). \]

This optimization problem is concave. The functions \(\ln \sigma(a_i)\) and \(\ln (1 - \sigma(a_i))\) are concave, so the log-likelihood term is concave. The term \(-\mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{a}/2\) is strictly concave, because \(\mathbf{K}\) is positive definite, which we assume so that \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\) exists. The sum is strictly concave, so the maximum is unique and global. The iteration converges to it for a small enough step \(\eta\).

The Hessian matrix gives the local curvature of the log posterior. For the diagonal elements of the likelihood term, the second derivative is \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial a_i^2} \sum_{j=1}^N [t_j \ln \sigma(a_j) + (1-t_j) \ln (1-\sigma(a_j))] &= \frac{\partial}{\partial a_i} (t_i - \sigma(a_i)) \\ &= -\sigma'(a_i) \\ &= -\sigma(a_i)(1-\sigma(a_i)). \end{aligned}\]

For the off-diagonal elements, each term in the sum depends on a single \(a_i\), so the mixed partial derivatives of the likelihood term are zero. The prior term \(-\mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{a}/2\) contributes \(\mathbf{K}^{-1}\). The Hessian of the negative log posterior at the mode is \[ \mathbf{H} = -\nabla_{\mathbf{a}}\nabla_{\mathbf{a}}^T \ln p(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t})|_{\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{a}_{\text{MAP}}} = \mathbf{W} + \mathbf{K}^{-1}, \] where \(\mathbf{W} = \text{diag}(\sigma(a_1)(1-\sigma(a_1)), \ldots, \sigma(a_N)(1-\sigma(a_N)))\) contains the second derivatives of the negative log-likelihood at \(\mathbf{a}_{\text{MAP}}\).

The Laplace approximation of the posterior is then \[ p(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) \approx \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{a}_{\text{MAP}}, \mathbf{H}^{-1}). \]

With a Gaussian approximation for \(p(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t})\), we can now carry out step 3 and compute the predictive distribution of the logit. It is the integral \[ p(a_*|\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) = \int p(a_*|\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{a}) p(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{a}. \]

Substituting the GP prediction of \(a_*\) given \(\mathbf{a}\) and the Laplace approximation gives \[ p(a_*|\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) \approx \int \mathcal{N}(a_*|\mathbf{k}_*^T \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{a}, k_{**} - \mathbf{k}_*^T \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{k}_*) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{a}_{\text{MAP}}, \mathbf{H}^{-1}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{a}. \]

The integral combines two Gaussians into another Gaussian, so that \[\begin{aligned} p(a_*|\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) &\approx \mathcal{N}(a_*|\mu_*, \sigma_*^2) \\ \mu_* &= \mathbf{k}_*^T \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{a}_{\text{MAP}} \\ \sigma_*^2 &= k_{**} - \mathbf{k}_*^T \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{k}_* + \mathbf{k}_*^T \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{k}_*. \end{aligned}\]

The gradient condition at \(\mathbf{a}_{\text{MAP}}\) simplifies the mean. The Woodbury identity of Equation 14.33, with \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{K}\), \(\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{V} = \mathrm{Id}\) and \(\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{W}^{-1}\), simplifies the variance. This gives \[\begin{aligned} \mu_* &= \mathbf{k}_*^T (\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{a}_{\text{MAP}})) \\ \sigma_*^2 &= k_{**} - \mathbf{k}_*^T (\mathbf{W}^{-1} + \mathbf{K})^{-1} \mathbf{k}_*. \end{aligned}\]

We now have the distribution of the logit \(a_*\), but step 4 needs the class probability, which is \[ p(t_*=1|\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) = \int \sigma(a_*) p(a_*|\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) \mathrm{d}a_*. \]

This integral has no closed form for the sigmoid. However, we can use the probit approximation of Section 9.6. It approximates the logistic sigmoid closely by the probit function \(\Phi(\lambda a)\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function and \(\lambda = \sqrt{\pi/8}\). This \(\Phi\) is unrelated to the design matrix \(\mathbf{\Phi}\).

Inserting this approximation into the integral and using the probit identity, we obtain \[ p(t_*=1|\mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{t}) \approx \sigma\left(\frac{\mu_*}{\sqrt{1 + \pi \sigma_*^2/8}}\right). \]

Interpreting the Class Probabilities

The factor \(1/\sqrt{1 + \pi \sigma_*^2/8}\) is an uncertainty moderation term. It is the same mechanism that we met in Bayesian logistic regression in Sections 9.6 and 9.7. When \(\sigma_*^2\) is large, for example far from the training data, the latent function is uncertain, and the factor shrinks \(\mu_*\) toward zero. The prediction then moves toward \(\sigma(0) = 0.5\), which is maximum uncertainty. Near many training points, \(\sigma_*^2\) is smaller, the factor is closer to 1, and the prediction is closer to \(\sigma(\mu_*)\). This moderation is an advantage of the full Bayesian treatment, because simpler methods can make overconfident predictions.

The mean \(\mu_* = \mathbf{k}_*^T (\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}(\mathbf{a}_{\text{MAP}}))\) is a weighted sum of the residuals at the training points. A training point whose label is far from the MAP prediction has a large residual and contributes more to the prediction at a new point. The weights are the kernel similarities \(\mathbf{k}_*\) between the new point and the training points. The residuals carry the correlations among the training points, because \(\mathbf{a}_{\text{MAP}}\) depends on the kernel matrix.

The variance \(\sigma_*^2 = k_{**} - \mathbf{k}_*^T (\mathbf{W}^{-1} + \mathbf{K})^{-1} \mathbf{k}_*\) has the form of the GP regression variance, with \(\mathbf{W}^{-1}\) in place of the noise covariance \(\mathbf{\Sigma}_n\). The matrix \(\mathbf{W}\) measures how sensitive each observation is to changes in the latent function. Points near decision boundaries carry the most information about where the boundaries lie, so they reduce the uncertainty the most.

14.13 Extending to Multiclass Classification

Many astronomical applications need more than two classes, for example stellar spectral types, galaxy morphologies or classes of variable stars. Can we extend Gaussian process classification beyond the binary case? Naive approaches such as one-vs-rest can give inconsistent decision boundaries and conflicting predictions where the binary classifiers disagree (Section 8.1). Astronomical applications that need uncertainty estimates require a coherent model whose probabilities sum to one and whose decision boundaries agree for all classes.

As with multi-class logistic regression, where Chapter 9 covers only the binary case, we opt out of a full Bayesian treatment of multiple classes. It is conceptually straightforward, but a few points need care, and we sketch them here. A complete development would need another chapter, which this book does not include.

The multinomial probit model extends the binary case to \(C\) classes, with a probit link in place of the sigmoid. It uses \(C-1\) latent functions, and one function is fixed to zero as the reference class. Each of the other functions is the score of class \(c\) relative to the reference class, with the prior \[ f_c(\mathbf{x}) \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_c(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')). \]

We can use the same kernel for all classes or give each class its own kernel to reflect class-specific characteristics. The class assignment follows the simple rule \[ t = \arg\max_c f_c(\mathbf{x}), \]where the maximum includes the reference class. This gives consistent decision boundaries by construction. The boundary between any two classes \(i\) and \(j\) is the set of points where \(f_i(\mathbf{x}) = f_j(\mathbf{x})\). The input space is therefore partitioned without gaps or overlaps. The class probabilities also sum to one, because one class wins.

The inference is more complex than in the binary case. With \(C-1\) functions and \(N\) training points, we must infer \((C-1) \times N\) latent variables simultaneously. The likelihood for a training point \((\mathbf{x}, t=c)\) is the probability that class \(c\) has the largest score, which is \[ p(t=c|\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})) = p(f_c(\mathbf{x}) > f_j(\mathbf{x}) \text{ for all } j \neq c). \]

This probability involves integrating over a truncated multivariate Gaussian distribution, which has no convenient closed form. Unlike the binary case, where the probit approximation gave closed-form solutions, the multiclass setting needs numerical approximations.

The Laplace approximation extends to this setting. We find the mode of the posterior over the latent variables and approximate the posterior by a Gaussian. Even then, the integrals that give the predictive class probabilities need additional approximations. The Hessian matrix of the Laplace approximation grows as \(\mathcal{O}((C-1)^2 N^2)\). For many classes and large \(N\), the memory and the computing time both become too large.

Nevertheless, for moderate problems that need uncertainty estimates, multiclass GP classification keeps the probabilistic treatment of the binary case. It expresses uncertainty about objects that fall between well-defined classes. Where misclassification has serious consequences, this can justify the additional computing.

The \(\mathcal{O}(N^3)\) cost of a Gaussian process limits its direct use to moderate problems, typically with fewer than several thousand observations. Approximation methods can scale Gaussian processes to larger data sets, and they remain an active area of research. Neural networks (Chapter 15) are another route to flexible nonlinear modeling. They scale to far larger data sets, but their uncertainty estimates need extra methods. Both approaches have been used in astronomy, and they can complement each other.

14.14 Tutorials: Stellar Light Curves and Star-Galaxy Classification

A Gaussian process (GP) infers a function from data without a fixed parametric form, and it states how well the data fix the function. Two tutorials use GPs, one for regression and one for classification. The first learns the timescale of stellar brightness variations from Kepler light curves. The second separates stars from galaxies by their Gaia colors. The full tutorials can be found at https://statml.org/ as 14a and 14b.

Timescales of Stellar Brightness

Convection and oscillations make the brightness of a star vary. The variations are slower in an expanded, evolved star of low surface gravity, \(\log g\), than in a compact one. A timescale measured from a light curve could therefore tell us how evolved a star is. The tutorial infers this timescale with a GP from Kepler light curves and compares it with the asteroseismic \(\log g\) of each star.

A fixed shape, such as a sinusoid, would decide in advance how the brightness varies. A GP with an RBF kernel (Section 14.3) assumes only that the brightness varies smoothly. Its length scale \(\ell\) is the time over which the brightness stays correlated, which is the timescale that we want.

Each star gets its own length scale, together with a noise level for the measurement errors (Section 14.7). We choose both by maximizing the marginal likelihood (Section 14.9). A short length scale lets the GP follow every wiggle, including the noise, and the marginal likelihood penalizes this extra flexibility. It thus balances the fit against the complexity of the model. In Figure 14.12a the fit to a star of low gravity traces its slow, smooth variations, and its length scale is long.

Across the stars, the length scale falls as the surface gravity rises (Figure 14.12b), as the slower variations of evolved stars predict. Calibrated on stars of known gravity, the length scale could estimate \(\log g\) from a light curve alone.

A GP describes a signal without fixing its shape in advance, and its kernel turns the data into quantities with a physical meaning. Here one number, the length scale, tracks how evolved a star is. The same approach models other signals of unknown shape, such as the variability of quasars or the stellar activity that hides planets.

Separating Stars from Galaxies

The second tutorial predicts a class instead of a number. Imaging surveys detect far more objects than spectroscopic surveys can observe, so we must separate stars from galaxies by photometry. Faint stars and galaxies have similar colors, the brightness differences between filters, so the classes overlap. An object near their border needs a probability, so that spectroscopy goes to the uncertain ones. The tutorial classifies faint Gaia sources of known class by their colors BP\(-\)RP and G\(-\)RP.

A straight line, as in logistic regression (Section 7.5), separates these classes poorly, because the stars lie on both sides of the galaxies. It misclassifies many of the test objects (Figure 14.13a). A GP classifier (Section 14.11) replaces the line by a latent function, a hidden score that the sigmoid turns into a probability. We give the latent function a GP prior, so that its boundary can bend around the galaxies. The likelihood of a label is not Gaussian, so the posterior of the latent function has no closed form. We approximate it by a Gaussian at its peak, the Laplace approximation, and the probit approximation then gives the probability (Section 14.12).

The length scale of the kernel sets how quickly the boundary can bend. The marginal likelihood has no closed form here, so we choose the length scale by cross-validation (Section 14.10). Cross-validation fits the classifier on part of the objects and tests it on the rest, for each length scale, and we keep the best one. The boundary then encloses the galaxies (Figure 14.13b), and most of the test objects are classified correctly.

With a much shorter length scale (Figure 14.13c), the boundary follows individual objects. The classifier then gets nearly all the training objects right but fewer test objects than the best length scale does. A much longer length scale makes the boundary too smooth and lowers the test accuracy as well.

The GP classifier gives a probability for each object. The probability is one half on the boundary. It also returns to one half far from every object (Figure 14.13b). There the kernel carries no information, and the probit approximation pulls uncertain predictions toward one half. An object with a probability near one half is therefore on the border or unlike the training objects. These are the objects to observe spectroscopically.

In both tutorials the kernel leaves the shape of the function open, and the length scale is what we must still learn. For the light curves it is a timescale, and the marginal likelihood finds it for each star. For the classifier it sets how quickly the boundary can bend, and cross-validation chooses it because the marginal likelihood has no closed form there. The cost of a GP grows quickly with the number of objects (Section 14.8), so it suits samples of hundreds to a few thousand objects. In return, a GP states what it does not know, as the probability that returns to one half far from the objects.

Aronszajn (1950) developed the theory of reproducing kernels, the mathematics behind kernel methods. Matheron (1963) and Cressie (1993) connected Gaussian processes to spatial statistics. O’Hagan (1978) gave a Bayesian treatment of curve fitting with GP priors. Kimeldorf and Wahba (1970) and Wahba (1990) related splines and smoothing to them. Rasmussen and Williams (2006) wrote the standard modern treatment. Neal (1996) showed that GPs are the limit of one-hidden-layer neural networks of infinite width. Csató and Opper (2002) and Snelson and Ghahramani (2005) developed sparse approximations that summarize the data with a few points. Quiñonero-Candela and Rasmussen (2005) gave a common view of them. Titsias (2009) chose these points by maximizing a lower bound on the likelihood. Foreman-Mackey et al. (2017) developed celerite, which computes one-dimensional Gaussian processes with suitable kernels in linear time, and applied it to stellar rotation and asteroseismology. Williams and Barber (1998) used the Laplace approximation for classification. Minka (2001) presented expectation propagation, another Gaussian approximation of the posterior, and Kuss and Rasmussen (2005) compared them. MacKay (1992) described the evidence method for hyperparameters. Kennedy and O’Hagan (2001) used GPs to calibrate computer models. Stein (1999) treated interpolation and the Matérn class. Aigrain and Foreman-Mackey (2023) review Gaussian processes for astronomical time series, from kernel choice and scalable computation to applications to exoplanets and active galactic nuclei. Hughes et al. (2022) classified Gaia sources as quasars, galaxies and stars with labels from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. The classes of the second tutorial follow their work.
